Author: @lvory92
Content:
Lossless Scaling is decent but it's not without its drawbacks. 
1) It works best when you already have a decent PC. Generating extra frames puts a strain on your hardware. If your computer has lower specs, it's not going the get the same gains...
2) The latency is noticeable. For users with KB+M, or playing shooters, it's not ideal. This can be improved by turning Vsync off but then you have to deal with visual tearing. 
3) There will be visual artifacts and ghosting. Since LS is a third party program, it cannot tell the UI apart from the rest of the scene, resulting in the aforementioned issues.

Ideally, you want developers to optimize their games so you don't have to rely on band-aid solutions to get good performance... or spend more money. Companies don't mind selling poorly optimized games because it's less work for them and it incentivizes people to buy newer hardware with all these newfangled AI solutions and newer FSR / DLSS versions... They create a problem to sell you the solution.

Author: @ilKamuTube
Content:
LSFG is an extraordinary technology for bringing frame generation everywhere, but — unlike DLSS 4’s MFG — it must wait for the completion of the real frame before generating the supplementary one.
This results in a minimum delay equal to one frame plus the software overhead. At 60 fps, where each frame lasts about 16.67 ms, LSFG adds roughly 16.67 ms of delay plus 2–4 ms of overhead, for a total of about 18.7–20.7 ms.
DLSS 4’s MFG on RTX 5000, on the other hand, calculates the extra frames in parallel with rendering, introducing only about 2–4ms of hardware overhead: overall latency remains very close to native rendering, and the difference is huge!

Content:
I tried this program before. Here is what i can say:
Framegen will decrease your actual framerate but will give you smoother image by giving you imput lag. And a noticable one. If you are used at your actual frames, then this imput lag will ruin your timings feeling. So, for 1st person games its pretty much unusable. HOWEVER, for strategies, or some not-action games it will give you free FPS. The controls will feel sluggish but youll get used to it. Also its GREAT instrument for old games. Because it can make 4 frame walking animation into 8, 16, or higher frames animation, making it much less clunky. 
Upscaling... didnt find any usage for it. Games that support FSR give up to +250% more FPS, while lossless scaling seems to add none. Same goes with other upscaling techs.

So, now I cap every 3rd person game I play at fixed 60 or 70 fps and use LSFG to 120 or 140..it gives me perfectly ruler flat frametime and the smoothest possible gaming experience with a controller.

Lossless Scaling feels like magic and looks and works way better than amd framegen (AFMF).

Author: @utasmasodik7726
Content:
There are probably working configs too, where this whole image generation nonsense is almost unnoticeable — especially considering the GPU is already doing the actual image generation. I really don’t get what else needs to be generated here, when it’s only been a few years since people even realized that games were running at 30 FPS on the PS4 (and even on the PS3 — not to mention other consoles).
So yeah, whoever came up with this is a “genius,” because it just keeps generating stuff and smooths out the frames in between, making things look more fluid ("but it’s still generated").
But if the motion that belongs to the character isn’t actually seen — even if the character appears in front of you — and something gets skipped and is just replaced, that doesn’t mean it’s really there.
Basically, out of the 100 things that should happen, the 30th frame in a single second gets generated 10 or 20 times before the 32nd — so instead of there being a real 31st frame, it’s just NOT THERE.
And what happens? GPU load is saved because it just copies the previous frame and blends it into the next.
SO: A frame is missing! 😄

And let’s be real: we’re already being tricked enough by games — I mean, we’re playing them after all! 😉😜
The concept is brilliant, sure...
But why should I play something that only pretends the frame is there, when in reality, it’s NOT THERE AT ALL!?

Also — sorry, but I honestly think game developers should tone down some of the things they cram into games that the average GPU simply can’t handle in a reasonable way.
Maybe they should start designing games in a way that doesn’t constantly push everything beyond limits.
And to be fair, if those limits hadn’t been pushed so hard in the first place, we probably wouldn’t even need a tool like this.
If games were better optimized from the start, this whole “frame generation magic” wouldn’t be necessary at all

Author: @blitzgear02
Content:
dual GPU is the meta with lossless scaling frame gen. sans CPU bottleneck and with solid base framerates, you can get believable eye candy fps on just about any game, *especially* ones that have their own framegen like space marine 2 or marvel rivals. I've been using an RX 9070 XT as my main powerhouse card and an RX 6600 as my secondary frame gen card... and there's nothing I haven't been able to run. completely rock solid.

fair warning though: If your system can't manage to get at least 45-80 FPS solid on the games you're trying to run at preferred settings, then framegen isn't going to compensate for your brutal input lag. it'll be a beautifully smooth slideshow instead of a regular slideshow. However, if you *can* hit 50-80? crank up the framegen to 2x or 3x and the added latency is basically negligible while getting double/triple the frames. it's really impressive what this setup can do. 

rec spec for secondary cards is 8 GB at the minimum for I believe 1080p @ 200hz and *maybe* 4K at a lower refresh rate? somewhere around 120? I'm not sure about the numbers but this is (to my knowledge) still a very young and more-art-than-science technique. In addition, make sure your system isn't RAM limited. This setup uses windows' "DWM" feature primarily and operates by passing frames between VRAMs via RAM. I've personally found that DDR4 @ 3200 MHz is adequately fast and isn't introducing any undue latency. Upgrading to DDR5 doesn't seem like a necessity to me, at least if you're trying to kit out an old rig with spare parts.

For additional context, the rig I've been running this on is an i7-11700F on a MPG Gaming Force Z590 mobo. 4x16GB DDR4 @ 3200 MHz (XMP) utilizing an RX 9070 XT in my PCIe 4.0 x16 and my RX 6600 in my PCIe 3.0 x16. Both cards are running at x8 speeds due to this mobo not having coveted bifurcation capabilities (and good luck ever finding them at consumer spec), but so far, I haven't had reason to suspect that the bandwidth on either card has harmed them in any way. I'm sure I could knock down a few %s as far as latency milliseconds go but I'm not *that* concerned. The i7 is the primary bottleneck in games but even that hasn't stopped this machine from being able to run just about everything, even handling Star Citizen admirably with LSFG's help using this technique. 

If you already have the parts laying around or just upgraded to the new GPUs and still have your old one, I highly recommend at least trying it. LSFG is extremely good on its own, but this combo feels like cheating. these are the most legitimate fake frames you will ever witness.

Author: @Ohmz27
Content:
I've been using Lossless for years, since before they added FG, the scaling features alone were more than worth the price tag. The Frame-gen wasn't the best, but since the 3.0 update it's been AMAZING. I had a 3090 and was using LSFG everywhere I could, even playing FPS with it. The plan was to upgrade to a 5000 series, but when they leaned towards AI, I figured I'd keep my 3090 and LSFG made this a far more comfortable decision. Games that I could comfortably play at high FPS, I found myself bumping up to max quality with a forced 60-80FPS limit and using LSFG to bump to 165FPS. This would keep gameplay perfectly smooth, lower GPU temps a tad, while letting me play at raised fidelity than if I was not using LSFG and tried to hit high FPS. My 3090 died recently, so I upgraded to a 5080. The 5000 series GPUs (perhaps 4k too) give access to a "Smooth Motion" feature, which is an out-of-engine driver enforced frame-gen for games that don't support DLSSFG. I was excited to give that a go, and honestly LSFG is far superior to nVidia's Smooth Motion in every possible way. It's MUCH easier to enable, MUCH more customizable, and even gave me way less artifacting too. Similar situation with RTX HDR and SpecialK too - the only time I'd use RTX HDR is if SpecialK could not be used (due to anti-cheats or compatibility issues etc).

DLSSFG is really cool though, and it's impressive that LSFG really isn't far-off.

Author: @themonlight13
Content:
9:10 Data rate does matter but it is highly dependent on the GPU you use, the PCI-E Gen that second slot offers (and how that second slot is connected, if its not directly connected to the CPU you will have problems with performance) and mayve a little bit the resolution you target in the end. If you have an 4.0 X8 card like the 4060 a 4.0 X4 Slot also works just fine. Also plugging your screen into the second GPU as described also has another big advantage - you dont need to copy the real and the generated frames back into the frame buffer of your primary GPU thus also reducing load on the PCI-E bandwith.

Also, Dual-GPU Setups (especially mixed ones with AMD and NVIDIA) tend to have problems in certain older games (blurred text), some DLSS-Titles (crashing) or the game selecting and sticking with the "wrong" GPU.

Author: @ChrisM-tn3hx
Content:
Bought this last night. Thanks for the tip, Linus!

I have a 4060 on my laptop (ASUS ROG G16), but still bought this for use with Cyberpunk, because the latest 2 patches have something wrong the drivers and on my specific model apparently it's a known issue that it will run the GPU until it overheats and then crash the system. Happened to me repeatedly. This solved the issue. I run a lower version than current, so the bug doesn't destroy my machine, and then run this in the background. 

The performance and visual difference is incredible, and I just played a 4-hour session without any hint of a heat issue.  I've got a 34-inch ASUS ultrawide, and had previously had to run Cyberpunk at a lower res than the monitor is capable of (1080 ultrawide instead of 1440 ultrawide) in order to maintain decent framerate. With this running, it upscaled to 1440 ultrawide no problem, and I ended up turning frame gen down to a static multiplier of 1.5 for performance sake. I can run it at 2 but after a couple of hours is slows down a bit and I have to restart. Not a problem with this software, it's the usual Cyberpunk memory leak over time. With it set to 1.5, 4 hours or so was no problem.  I was even able to turn up a couple of settings for things like reflections.

It's literally like playing a brand new game. Especially in rain.

Author: @drskelebone
Content: HUD motion should be trivially fixable.  The upscaler should keep count of the "sum" and the "variance" of each pixel over time.  HUD pixels don't change, resulting in a large sum and low variance.  This can then be converted into a "render mask" that excludes those pixels from the interpolation process and ensures that they're left undisturbed post processing.  I'm saying this is an algorithmic issue, and one that could be fixed quickly if the team wasn't "one dude."  Congrats to that One Dude, though.  Impressive.

Author: @creationsmaxo
Content:
The one thing that native scaling GPU tech has (which explain how some stuff look uglier, but some looks sharper) is an access to the Z-Buffer of the game engine.
What this means is that it's possible for the GPU, when applying upscaling, to focus primarily on stuff closer to the player. You can convert the Z-Buffer of a game engine into a grayscale texture and from this texture, you can determine what's close or far in a really convenient 0.00 to 1.00 (or 0 to 256 depending on the grayscale encoding) comparison. Then it's also possible to modify this Z-Buffer with additional stuff to make the GPU focus on the right stuff and less on the "background decorative stuff". For example, you can hook up the upscaling AI to the LoD (Level of Detail) distance analytics system which would tell the GPU to only put limited resources to the stuff that is rendered as less detailed by said LoD. 

Hence, for stuff in the environment (like the chains), the upscale might be less focused on while the tree and other elements that may come into close range of the player could be more focused on.

To put it in a easy-to-imagine perspective, imagine that the frame is a painting done with brush strokes. With Lossless Scaling, the number of brush strokes is more or less stable across the whole painting because it's accessing and analyzing the whole frame. With the integrated scaling, it's as if the element closer to the player (or set as more important in the engine) are getting more brush strokes than the stuff that is further or less important.

Author: @Demising
Content: A few things to note is that for one, the frame generation benefits more with a higher base frame rate as it has more frames to look through to calculate and make the interpolated frames. Ghosting and UI wobbling aren't as noticeable at say 60fps 2x scaled to 120fps, versus 30fps 4x scaled to 120fps. Another thing with the FSR is Lossless Scaling uses FSR 1, as FSR 2 and onwards are directly implemented into the game (Spatial Upscaling vs Temporal Upscaling), so each will provide different advantages and disadvantages, like the lack of ghosting on the latern from LSFSR versus the implemented FSR in Doom, and the tree textures.

Author: @Dankamidas
Content:
OptiScaler is a free, low-latency upscaling and frame generation tool for DirectX 11+ games. It offers more features and lower overhead than commercial alternatives like Lossless Scaling, making it ideal for improving performance in single-player games.

I make tutorial videos on how to install and configure it step by step. It's surprisingly easy once you know how.

⚠ Warning: Because OptiScaler hooks directly into the game’s rendering pipeline (similar to ReShade), it can trigger anticheat systems in multiplayer games and may get you banned. Stick to single-player titles or use the tool in linus's video here unless you fully understand the risks.

Author: @BigNSleepy
Content:
Welp, because of this video I went and bought it. Running an older near-potato spec PC. Ryzen 5600G + RX6400. I tested it on GTA online which I usually play at about medium quality, it was stable 60 frames but if I cranked it up it wasn't abnormal to see it get 18-22fps (1080p). Keeping it native resolution and adding the fixed 2x boost with a frame cap at 30, I plugged my primary monitor (dual monitor setup) into the motherboard and set the Vega 7 (igpu) to handle the frame generation and display output and the rx6400 to handle the workload, and to my absolute astonishment I got a stable 60 fps with a 0.1% low of 59 at ultra settings 1080p (no ray tracing) and the fidelity is picture perfect with no input lag. Its as if im playing it on a considerably nicer pc! Also, on top of that, Im using 10-15% less GPU, less VRAM, and instead of my igpu sitting idle or at 5-10% (because its doing the display now) it kicks up to 45-55%. GPU uses 27w and the APU combo uses around a combined 50w tops when its night time and everything is reflecting. 

TLDR: If you have a lower-end 1080p rig that can't quite get the job done, and you've got an integrated gpu or an old second one laying around it is ABSOLUTELY worth buying Lossless Scaling.

Author: @Omili
Content:
Playing Skyrim with 4000 mods maxed out graphics and so on. My computer has 4070ti and I get around 30 fps in major city like Whiterun that has tons of NPCs, trees, buildings, moving objects and physics objects + every character around me have HDT/SMP hair and clothing physics. Game is playable and when I go outside of the city or go in to any smaller interior like a cave, the FPS jumps to around 60-80.

When I put Lossless scaling on (I have not tested anything else than fixed 3.1 with default settings) I get around 90 to 160 fps and the input lag feels very low / non existent almost all the time. However after 2 hours or so I need to reboot Skyrim because it slows down constantly due to massive amounts of mods and things happening and saving data. Anyone who have played ultra modded Skyrim knows what it feels like without beast computer. Lossless scaling works really well for Skyrim and for many other games too. Some games however do not work well with it and usually have way too high input lag or less FPS than without the app.

Definetly worth the asking price.

Content: Worth noting that there's an open source Linux port called lsfg-vk being made too, and it uses Vulkan as the renderer. It still requires the original to use the libraries from it, which is good because supporting devs that make great stuff is important.

Author: @VoxelMusic
Content:
LS frame gen does have some automatic HUD detection but it relies on your "Flow Scale". When the flow scale is set too low, you get that warping effect on the crosshair.
Also, the LS upscaling is all spatial, so itll be lower quality than built in FSR but with zero ghosting.
Lastly, you had "Performance Mode" enabled on LSFG through the entire video which dips the framegen quality.

Author: @altairfoo1920
Content:
It is a pretty neat software. But the image upscaling are not really the selling point it unless the GPUs are EOLed. They are spatial upscalers not temporal upscalers(AMD FSR2/3/4, DLSS, UE5 TSR, etc...). So people with a relatively modern GPU can actually just enable the upscaling in their control panel.
But the frame gen option is still pretty good regardless of the obvious issue of unable to mask the UI (for now). And btw, it is not really AMD or NV that "hand tune" the FG for games, they simply require a UI-less buffer from the game engine, FG it, and then composite back into the chain.

Content:
Lossless scaling has been a must have for me.   I use it for most games i play from Space Marines 2 to older games through emulation. The profile I use , I hope this helps anyone interested:
-Frame Generation
Type:  LSFG 3.1
Mode:  Fixed
Multiplier:  2
Flow Scale:  around 80%
Performance:  Off

-Scaling
Type:  Off
Mode:  Auto  -  Fullscreen

-Rendering
Sync mode:  Vsync
Max frame latency:  1
HDR support:  Off
G-Sync support:  Off
Draw FPS:  On

-Capture
Capture API:  DXGI  (not able to upgrade to windows 11 so cant say how good WGC is)
Queue target:  0

-Cursor
All:  off

-GPU & Display
All:  Auto

-Crop Input
All:  0

-Behavior
Multi-display mode:  On

Author: @georgemathiellis5486
Content:
I think you missed the mark by focusing on mainstream titles—games where visual detail is mostly cosmetic and you're already pushing 50+ FPS. Of course it's hard to notice quality loss when you’re dealing with eye candy and excess frames.

Try something like DCS in VR, where both frame rate and image clarity directly affect gameplay. You need to read cockpit gauges, spot distant targets, and react in real time—fake frames and artifacts aren't just minor issues, they're dealbreakers.

We desperately need smoother performance in VR sims, but not at the cost of clarity. That’s where AI-generated frames fall apart. If you want to properly test this tech, pick games where visual fidelity isn't optional—where it actually matters.

Author: @Xbob42
Content:
22:00 Well, not quite. I don't think it was ever really meant to boost really bad FPS to good. It, as far as I know, has always been about taking an FPS that's alright-but-not-quite-there and making it really good. I get why people would automatically assume it's for boosting very low FPS, but that's when it works the worst because there's simply not enough data to work with. Always remember to leave a little GPU overhead as well, not just with Lossless Scaling, but any of these solutions. If that means lowering a couple settings, that's fine, because it keeps your base FPS higher. As they say in the video, it's not free to do this, so if your GPU is at 99%, then you're gonna chunk way into your native FPS. So keep as high as a native FPS as you can without maxing out your GPU, and you'll achieve far superior results.

That's not to say it can't, say, boost a 30 FPS game to 60. I think Okami for example is a lot more enjoyable with Lossless Scaling 2x, but in those cases you're gonna want relatively slow games at a completely stable 30 FPS, since they'll suffer least from artifacting.

Author: @wesleykim1758
Content:
Something to note is that if you want the best performance you need to limit your frames in game and then set a multiplier, not use adaptive.

When you limit your frames you ensure a more consistent framerate which allows for smoother frame generation, and since you aren't chasing a target framerate with adaptive it only multiplies by whatever framerate it is given. This is because the amount of processing power is similar between partial and full integer scaling options, so a 2.28x multiplier might be the equivalent of a 3x multiplier. Meaning if you want to get more performance you should use integer scaling to avoid unnecessary increases in processing power

For example, I run Expedition 33 on 4k native and limit frames to 30fps and add an 8x multiplier to hit ~240fps. While my GPU can get higher than that, 30fps is what I can hit consistently and after some tweaks I can consistently hit 240fps with minimal lag and artifacting. Its not perfect, but between playing at 45fps and 240fps on a game where input lag is not a huge issue, Id rather have the smoother gameplay.

Also, fun thing to do is watch YouTube with Lossless scaling, you can frame gen a video to get it smoother than the 60fps limit which can be a bit freaky since everything and people seem to glide around the screen when it works well

Author: @AetherProwl
Content: The FSR built into the game is FSR 2 which is temporal based, the one in lossless scaling is just FSR 1 which is spacial based. FSR 1 is cool because it doesn’t have any ghosting or shimmering issues and can be implemented into literally anything as a screen space filter without any kind of app integration. They have it in the AMD driver now as RSR. Down side is that without temporal accumulation, it’s not going to get anywhere close to native image quality, and will amplify any artifacts present in the native image.

Content: Glad to see this getting some attention from LTT.  It's a great bit of software and worth every penny.  It's also got some utility outside of just "more frames."  One of my favorite uses of it is in Kerbal Space Program.  If I run that game at my native 4K resolution, all the HUD elements, context menus and (especially) info presented on the map screen are too small because the game doesn't scale them correctly for the resolution.  Lossless Scaling lets me run the game at 1440P and scale it to 4K.  In terms of image quality the difference is negligible, but it's MUCH better to play because it scales all of those small text elements.

Author: @accelerationnation8171
Content:
HELLDIVERS PSA
I use this tool when playing HD2 all the time (hundreds of hours) and it can be very helpful, BUT consider the following:
1. HD2 tends to be a bit more CPU limited than GPU limited, especially on higher game difficulties, so improvements in fps will vary upon the quality of your CPU relative to your GPU.
2. Flashing lights and very sudden color changes tend to be a problem with the current version of lossless scaling, this becomes especially obvious when you see bullet trails, muzzle flashes from the gatling sentry, etc.
3. If you don't configure the settings correctly then the input latency can be TERRIBLE, I personally recommend limiting your fps using Riva Tuner Statistics alongside MSI Afterburner to solve this issue. Look up a guide online if you need help getting the settings right.

Author: @dwatts64
Content:
Something important to know: what you're playing will have a HUGE impact on the quality of interpolated frames. Doom: The Dark Ages is kind of a best case scenario for Lossless Scaling, so it works beautifully, but then something like Final Fantasy XVI or the new Wuchang: Fallen Feathers looks awful. Lossless scaling really struggles with grass, foliage, and other irregular patterns or "noisy" environments, just like Nvidia and AMD's solutions do. So you really need to configure your settings on a case by case basis, and some games just don't play as nicely as others. In my experience I have found that Unreal 5 games are the most hit or miss games for Lossless Scaling. It's either really great, or really bad, hardly ever in between. 

Also, because Lossless Scaling is essentially the last step in the pipeline, it is also including the HUD in any interpolation or upscaling it's doing, so you might notice some warbles, wiggles, and artifacts around stuff like your health bar or crosshair when you move the camera quickly.

Author: @thom1218
Content: For anyone interested in untangling the marketing word-games:  It's true that when you up-scale you don't "lose" anything, even just simple linear upscaling is "lossless" - but the whole point of up-scaling is to "add" more information in the form of enhanced detail, which can only be approximated by the training of the neural net used to do the up-scaling.  This isn't the future where the labcoat tech says "enhance" and the photo goes from pixelated to full original detail... it's AI hallucinated detail - and that's where this comes in - on the AI hype train.

Content: I found that even with a refresh rate and capabilities to well exceed 60fps, the smoothest results I've found with Lossless Scaling was using BCAS upscaling with adaptive frame generation target set to 126 (the additional frames compensate for possible base frame rate drops, keeping the actual scaled rate at 120fps solid). You need to be able to run at least 50fps for 100fps target or 60 for 120fps target and if you can get past 60 but not quite 120, lossless scaling can generate and fill in the rest and the less generated frames it has to make, the better your image quality and input latency will be. For my system, not enabling the frame generation performance toggle or lowering flow scale gives what seems like a 1:1 native image with only a few hardly noticeable evidence of upscaling/frame interpolation. You can have very good latency if you really know how it works.

Author: @WallaWaller
Content:
For people that want to use this, keep in mind it isn't intended to go beyond using a 1080p input image, which is 50% flow scale at 4k. In reality the program works incredibly well at more moderate resolutions. The 8700G iGPU can handle tripling 55fps to 165 when using a 1080p input image, and this is my primary use for the program. Truth be told most people would find great value if they could either buy or find an RX 580 GPU or equivalent. What's nice is that vRAM isn't even that big a deal since you aren't going beyond maybe 4gb even when processing a 4k image.

With all this said it's not perfect, and IMO isn't not worth it if you can get a native 80+fps as the added input latency is an issue. It's also not worth it if your framerate is under 40, because Lossless Scaling adds its own input latency of about 1/2 of a frame, meaning your 60fps feels like 45, and 40fps feels like 30 with input lag. This decreases as framerate increases but ultimately if you can get beyond 80 you're better off just not dealing with input latency at all.

Content:
As someone who used LS for some games. If your GPU can not hit like 25 to 30ish fps. Probably dont try it especially in games with a lot of HUD (looking at 3D Gachas)

Generally another thing to note. If you are required to make many quick movements in secession, you will notice the artifacting and the smudging much more. 

Ideally as Linus tested, use LS in single player games because the input lag is noticeable. Online/Competitive games thay require the least amount of input lag should not use this software.

The ideal FPS threshold as Linus noted is somewhere between 60 and your ideal FPS (like 120 or 144). 

If your GPU already supports Frame Gen, please use those instead. 

Also I HIGHLY RECOMMEND THAT IF YOU BUY THIS, LOOK UP A GUIDE OM HOW TO CONFIGURE IT. They made this look somewhat simple but its a very complicated software if you wanna optimize it

Author: @dragosalexpop
Content: LSFG user here: when you scale from 1080 to native, you need to cap the FPS at the monitor's refresh rate. That way you eliminate that excessive tearing. You can cap it in the GPU control panel or ingame menu or wherever. LSFG shines at making older games that have engines which don't support 60fps or more, much more playable. Take Command and Conquer Generals, or Lord of the Rings Battle for Middle Earth. Both are EA games using the SAGE engine. That engine is capped at 30fps so no matter what you do, if you crank it to ultra and have lots of units in play, you will get lower than 30 fps and thus making it unbearable. This is where LSFG will make your experience extremely satisfying, since you don't actually need to care that much about latency or HUD elements, because they always stay fixed.

Author: @TheJayBee1990
Content:
I use Lossless Scaling since Release now. And its great, when used right. There are games like FPS, Just Cause, Hogwarts Legacy, Shooter in general, where I wouldnt recommend using frame gen. I use this a lot in Watch Dogs 2. The extra details setting is really taxing in that game. So I cap the FPS at 30 and use lossless scaling to boost it to 60fps. works like a charm and looks absolutely stunning in that game. But where I really see this app as a game changer: Building Games. Cities Skylines or Anno really profit from this. huge maps and cities in both games can really cripple you performance. fix the fps at a manageable rate like 30fps. Use LSFG 3.1, mode fixed, multi 2, flux scale around 35-40%; performance off. In Jurassic World Evolution 2 this actually renders the game possible to play for me. I have a huge park that really hits the performance of my pc. in runs around 28fps fixed when the park is closed. Due to lossless scaling I am able to actually enjoy the game in 60fps and it looks really good.

PS: another cool thing, any fullscreen video can use frame gen as well. wanna see ALL youtube videos with 60fps? No problem. I tried a movie with this. Episode III looks so smooth using this. totally remmoned it for the price!

Author: @jamescampbell8482
Content:
A base of 90 frames per second is the sweet spot for frame generation in this program provided you only want to double or triple the frames.

I personally use this program every day on my LCD so that I can actually benefit from backlight strobing since ULMB requires that the frame rate never drops below the refresh rate of the panel to benefit from ULMB.

My monitor is an overclocked BenQ XL 2720 1080P 144Hz running at 180 frames per second with strobe. 

I get a motion resolution of 1200 pixels per second in any game . It's fantastic, and is quite literally the best seven dollars you could spend on steam in my opinion.

I use a custom resolution of 3200 x 1800 get it locked to 90 in the one percent lows and then double. No artifacts that are notable because the persistence is only 5 1/2 ms per frame at 180 Hz and I've got a 50% duty cycle on the strobe so it's more like 2 ms of persistence. and input lag at 90 native frames is damn near perfect.

Linus was mentioning that motion wasn't good given the low quality of generated frames, I am telling you combine it with ULMB, and you will not say that.

When frame visibility time is at about 2 ms per frame, the artifacting that you notice around the Hud is much harder to notice

Author: @Torbjorn.Lindgren
Content: Now cover OptiScaler which allows running any of XeSS/FSR2/FSR3/FSR4*/DLSS* on pretty much any upscaler enabled title (the stars is for "on supported HW") and likewise bridges the gap between all the frame-generation techs. Example: The game only support FSR2, OptiScaler will allow you to actually run DLSS, XeSS, FSR4 or FSR3 instead (all superior to massively superior upscalers). Or with newer games and card, swap FSR3/4 for DLSS or vice-versa depending on which card you have, regardless of what the game supports. Obviously there can be issues with some games and they officially recommend NOT using this with online games since the "Injection" can trigger, well, various anti-cheat measures. That's far less likely to be an issue with Lossless Scalling since it plugs in way closer in the display chain - but that's also why it doesn't have motion vector which will degrade the result from any temporal upscaling solution activated using LS.

Author: @mbrj3idi830
Content:
It's a great and my best buy software oat. It's great for single player games, unsupported with (dlss,fsr) or old locked games, emulators & videos (YouTube, movies..etc). I don't recommend for eSport or online games.
But you can't mention it without dual-gpu setup. While it's not a must, but it works really nice in some cases. You can combine any two gpus, but AMD shines with it. I use 7900xt (for render) + 5600xt (frame generation using LS). It gives the main gpu more room (you can use it @ 100% without impacting latency or base frames). And this combination gives a less latency than dlss and fsr. But with some compromising, the second gpu will be the only one connected to monitors, you will have the second gpu features only (let's say 5070ti + 6600xt), you will be connected through 6600xt only and will lose some features that control the monitors from 5070ti because it's not connected anymore. Also, you need motherboard has another pcie slot runs at least @ gen3.0 x4 or higher, or m.2 to pcie adapter may work in some cases.

Author: @BucephalusHume
Content:
Im dissappointed by your coverage of this. I expected better from LTT. This software gets shilled hard, and no one appraises it properly. 

If you have a card or game that can't do frame gen with your GPU manufacturers version, this software is great. 

But LTT like everyone else, completely undersells the impact to your base/native framerate. 15% headroom is not enough! 15% is maybe the threshold for 'playable'. But I've seen Lossless Scaling eat up as much as 30% for just 2x framegen. 

Long story short: use this if a game is hard locked to a certain framerate or you cant use your manufacturers framegen or upscaling. Dont use a second gpu for this, use that money to just buy a better gpu. 

Even at 2x, if you use this on a game that doesnt naturally have gpu headroom, you base framerate can drop by as much as 40%. And no, limiting the framerate to artifically create headroom wont fix this. 

Impressive program, well done to the creator. But the creator and content creators covering this software need to be honest about what it actually does. It is nowhere near the quality of nvidia framegen and DLSS

Well to be honest, both Nvidia and AMD exaggerated about the complexity of upscaling / FSR. Especially their first versions were just pixel stretching/averaging with a bit of smartness built in. Content: I believe lossless scaling uses fsr 1 which is a spatial only technique, meaning it only considers data from one frame. It basically has to guess what the high res image looks like based on surrounding pixels. If you enable fsr in game its likely using fsr 3, which can use data from previous frames to construct more fine and accurate detail, but using data from previous frames has the downside of very noticeable ghosting in some scenarios.

Author: @akiwiwithaface8911
Content:
I’ve found that in driver (I’ve been using AMD’s driver frame gen) is particularly useful in games that lock to 60 fps (especially in my strange, self imposed, situation. See below). While many of these games will have ini fixes or mods, sometimes they will cause issues like changing the game speed, stuttering, tearing and sometimes even removing the modification if you open the settings menu. 

Particular to my janky ass set up, I have a weird power strip which my set up is plugged into where it has a “master plug” and “master controlled plugs”. I have my monitor plugged into the master plug and speakers and second monitor plugged into the master controlled plugs so that I don’t need to have my pc on to use my main monitor with the speakers. Normally this works without a problem; however, for whatever reason, when the monitor goes to 60hz mode ( which happens in a lot of these older games in full screen if they don’t have a borderless windowed mode) the monitor must not be pulling enough power to keep the other plugs on because the power strip clicks and the speakers and second monitor shut off. Now, is the simple solution to this to simply buy another power strip? Yes. However, I’m lazy and I’d probably be using the frame gen anyway because it actually works quite nicely since the input lag isn’t quite as jarring when it’s generating frames from 60 fps as opposed to 30-40. I think I’ll try out lossless scaling’s implementation since amd’s driver frame gen can be kinda janky and doesn’t have many settings.

Content:
I've tinkered with the Lossless Scaling app a bit on a very-old Windows 10 system that is stuck with a 2GB GT710. With such an old rig, I can very much feel the need for some extra overhead for the Lossless Scaling app. If something already ran at a playable rate, it was generally able to improve things. If it wasn't basically playable when clean, Lossless Scaling could actually make it worse. That was just a test case with an ancient card really, and I know that my newer system would more than have room to run Lossless Scaling along with the games. Kinda an ironic situation where my new system doesn't actually need the help, so I just don't think to use the Lossless scaling app. My fps greed isn't strong enough I guess.

Way back during the GPU shortages, the ancient GT710 gpu was livable at 720p, and one of those Marseille mCable kept me from having to have anti-aliasing turned on. The cable is only a sharp upscaler, but all these modern gpu scalers just weren't a thing yet.

Content: From my experience using LS, it's best to get your game's base FPS stabilized at a consistent 60 FPS with a capped frametime. You can use MSI Afterburner and RivaTuner to achieve this. I have an RX 6750 XT, Doom: The Dark Ages is quite demanding at 1440p with medium-high settings and in-game FSR set to Quality. However, with LS, I'm able to play most recent AAA titles at 1440p and 120 FPS. Again, the base framerate is capped at 60 FPS.

Author: @BlindFury
Content:
A couple tips for anyone wanting to use Lossless Scaling. 
It works best with a high base frame rate. 
Use frame gen at no more than 3x.
Lock your game's fps.
For example if you have a 144hz display lock your fps to 72 and put FG on 2x. If you have a 240hz lock it to 80 fps and use 3x.
That assuming your base fps isn't much higher than what you're locking it to. If you can maintain 120 lock it to that and double it to 240 than obviously do that instead.

Also try it out on movies. It's kinda crazy.

Author: @wowieiwwie
Content: AMD cards work way better as lossless scaling secondary GPU's than Nvidia cards.  I believe the best cheap card you can buy for this is an RX 6600XT, it's unbelievably incredible at lossless scaling, around 2.5x better tested frame gen than the RTX 3060.  Also if you run you game at a locked 60fps, then frame gen up to a higher amount, the input delay is almost a non issue.  I am not sure why people frame gen from an uncapped frame rate below 60fps because that is where you will run into frame pacing/delay issues, to the point where it's not worth using frame gen at all.  I recently built my setup with this technology in mind, so I run a 9060XT (which has the capability to run almost every title at 60fps), and a RX 580 to frame gen from 60 to 180fps.  I use lossless scaling for every game, almost zero delay/artifacting issues (it's there, but very very subtle).  It's nice playing Elden ring at 180 fps lol
